fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"Steel Manning the Reset Claim","body":"Chance Garton recorded this episode alone, with roughly 15,000 words of notes and more than 150 images, in order to answer a 72 minute livestream called Asylums Kirkbride's Dream by the channel Lucius Aurelion, which had been sent to him as the good research on the subject. He said the burden of proof sits with whoever makes the claim, that his sources were primary documents rather than history books, and that he would try to improve the other side's argument before addressing it. He also admitted the topic annoyed him, and that stripping his real feelings out of an earlier draft killed his motivation."},{"title":"Suspicions That Explain Themselves","body":"Fergus Falls in Minnesota went up between 1888 and 1912, with photographs showing the central tower unfinished in 1906 and complete by 1910. Buffalo State was built in phases from 1871 to 1896, opened in 1880 with only one wing, and sat through a ten year halt during an economic depression. Chance Garton argued that the genre keeps stating the answer to its own mystery: naming the daguerreotype while calling a blurry photo suspicious, calling Kirkbride's small tombstone odd after noting he came from an old Quaker family, and treating whited out skies as tampering when orthochromatic emulsion simply overexposed blue light."},{"title":"A Tenth of One Percent","body":"Against the claim that asylums held people who remembered a lost civilization, Chance Garton ran the arithmetic. About a dozen asylums operated in 1850, when census figures put the institutionalized population between 2,000 and 5,000 out of roughly 20 million Americans. By 1890 that figure had grown to about 74,000 out of 62 million, still around a tenth of one percent. He credited industrialization, urbanization, and the shift of care from family and church to the state, and pointed to Pliny Earle's book The Curability of Insanity and to firsthand patient memoirs showing that many people did walk back out."},{"title":"Numbered Iron Stakes and Rotted Wood","body":"Lucius Aurelion presented the large cemeteries as possible evidence of extermination centers. Chance Garton took the Milledgeville, Georgia figure of 25,000 burials and spread it across 168 years of operation, roughly 150 a year at an institution that by the 1960s held over 12,000 patients. He cited archaeology at the Mississippi State Lunatic Asylum in Jackson, where ground penetrating radar suggests as many as 7,000 bodies across about 20 acres, and New York's own estimate of 55,000 anonymous graves. Markers disappeared because inmates pulled numbered iron stakes in the 1960s and painted wooden stakes rotted in the damp climate."},{"title":"Receipts From the State Legislatures","body":"There was no federal asylum program, Chance Garton argued, because President Franklin Pierce vetoed Dorothea Dix's public land bill on May 3, 1854, leaving each state to fund its own. In Missouri, Callaway County won the Fulton asylum with a bid of $11,500 and 500 acres, and contractor Solomon Jenkins tendered $47,450 before running past $50,000, itemizing a steam engine, 900 feet of iron pipe, and a lodge for 24 patients. Iowa appropriated $125,000 for Independence in 1868, and the Buchanan County Bulletin printed a full list of local donors on May 8, 1868."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Tartaria reset theorists says 1800s insane asylums were dug up and repurposed to become concentration camps. Can we trust them?
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: This episode checks every claim made by a very popular creator in the Old World Reset genre. I dig for all possible records on 19th century insane asylums, the Kirkbride plan and Kirkbride buildings. We look at construction photos for Fergus Falls and Buffalo State, the mass graves at Milledgeville and the Mississippi State Lunatic Asylum, Franklin Pierce's 1854 federal asylum program veto, the Independence Iowa paper trail with named architects, stonemasons, and donor lists, on-site brickmaking from glacial clay, and the chemistry of vanilla skies in old photographs.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Asylum Look Predates Kirkbride", "body": "The staggered wings and central block that the reset channels treat as a worldwide signature trace back to the pavilion plan of British and French hospital design, visible in the Royal Naval Hospital at Plymouth in the late 1700s. Chance walks a chain of books that all predate Kirkbride, including Philippe Pinel's Treatise on Insanity from 1801, Samuel Tuke's account of the York Retreat, Esquirol's survey of every asylum in France, and John Connolly's 1847 volume on asylum construction, which already carries architectural plates seven years before Kirkbride published. Kirkbride did not originate the idea, he codified the American version of it."}, {"title": "A Paper Trail Across Two Continents", "body": "Governor Haight of California commissioned Dr. Edmund Wilkins to personally inspect 149 asylums across the United States, Canada, England, Scotland, Ireland, Belgium, France, Holland, Italy, the German states and Switzerland, then file the whole thing as a public report. In Sydney, Dr. Frederick Norton Manning toured Derby, Lancashire, Bethlehem, York and a long list of American institutions before he designed anything. Iowa's own 1869 commissioners cited the New South Wales study tour by name. An Australian toured the world's asylums and Iowans knew about it, and that kind of cross corroboration would have to be forged in dozens of archives at once."}, {"title": "Self Defeat Runs Through the Genre", "body": "Cumberland Hospital in Sydney genuinely was a repurposed building, the Parramatta Female Factory of 1818, designed by a transported convict forger named Francis Greenway, and the channel showing it never noticed the gift it had been handed. The Paris print of Bicetre offered as evidence of Kirkbride spreading across the lands was engraved by a man who died in 1754, roughly a century too early to prove anything. Rockwood in Ontario was raised with prison labor and limestone quarried on the prison property. Every example meant to prove a hidden worldwide plan arrives carrying its own ordinary explanation."}, {"title": "The Fake Looking Photograph Explained", "body": "The Bethlem entrance gates image dated 1896, the one held up as proof that old photographs were painted rather than taken, is not a straight photograph at all. It comes from The Queen's London, a large format volume of roughly 370 views produced by the halftone process, where a photograph is screened through a fine dot pattern so it can run on a letterpress beside type. Zoom in and the dots are visible. The copy circulating online had then been rescanned through several generations and saved as a GIF, piling dither on dither. Strange texture, ordinary Victorian printing technology."}, {"title": "Callan Park and the Colonial Boom", "body": "New South Wales spent 250,000 pounds on Callan Park, the largest and most expensive public works project the colony had yet attempted, and named its centerpiece the Kirkbride Block even though the pavilion layout is not a Kirkbride at all. A wool and gold export economy financed by British banking capital made that budget possible, sandstone quarried on site kept the material bill down, and gold rush arrivals who never struck it rich supplied much of the population. The building itself was sold as the medicine, and the original 666 bed capacity was overrun within a decade."}]
